title: Assignment Two
text:
R-generated graphic [via given code sample]





Online-generated graphic [proper names capitalized]


In practice, they both have the same information and basic toggle features, though the online version seems more condensed. Both were about equally user-friendly, once I finally got the gTrendsR package installed and Google stopped blocking my requests.
The difference is mostly versatility and specificity: the online portal is better for quick visual reference, whereas the R package has more options for toggling size, appearance, and labels. I’d use the latter for a research project or conference proposal.
The R package is also nice because you can selectively add more information and it arranges nicely into a dataframe. The CSV file that auto-downloads from Google Trends only has a date and relative number of hits for each search term, whereas the R package added columns for geotag and categorization. You can download these as separate CSV files online, but merging them would be tedious and could corrupt the data.

title: DataFrame Writeup
text:
This episode [“Delivering Smarter Cities & Better Public Policy w/ Data,” February 2022] was a conversation with Kaveh Vessali, a consultant at PwC Middle East working on digital transformation and smart cities. What immediately struck me was his eclectic professional background, which spanned urban planning to Silicon Valley to the State Department to consulting. As a grad student with a lot of disparate interests, it’s nice to see that bridging different industries actually isn’t a pipe dream, and people do merge these skills successfully and productively.
The discussion was mainly Vessali’s career, and then the connection between data and public policy. (I chose this episode because it had a clear connection to EPPS philosophy, and my interest in data science for policy research). The main point, that more and “bigger” data doesn’t change the fundamental “dimensions of life” or core policy considerations, was well-taken. At least in my own limited research experience, “big data” is only novel in method and application, not core theoretical questions. I fully resonate with his suggestion that we should train public policymakers to pragmatically leverage data for specific use-cases, not pour into an “army of [data] specialists” who don’t understand the practical application of their skills.
I am a bit curious about his proposal to develop “ground-up data-informed communities,” especially given the pragmatic constraints he mentions later on. Some of the key steps he mentions, like “baseline data literacy” or training up policymakers, imply some amount of existing data, resources, and people to work with. His suggestion to tailor data to business priorities, likewise, suggests existing business priorities, which are presumably somewhat informed by data. Of course, this is a chicken-egg problem that may be moot in practice, since nothing is presumed to exist in a vacuum.

title: Assignment Five
text:
For the most part, this code was very easy to run, though it certainly helps that the doc IDs are already provided to us!

Difficulties encountered:

rjason not available for my version of r, and I could not find a version to download online, so I did it with the CSV method instead. Strangely, R later nagged me for not installing rjason and installed it for me.
I also didn’t realize that working/saving directory names are case-sensitive and initially couldn’t figure out where my downloads saved to. Similarly, I thought it would automatically create a new folder, and was surprised when a large number of files randomly populated my “Documents” bar.

Usability: I’m actually not sure what my next step would be (technically/methodologically speaking) if I wanted to do a text analysis. It’s nice to have them as a PDF, but I wouldn’t know how to get it into a dataframe without OCR or some other scanning tool. A lot of them also have unconventional formatting that would be confusing to a robot reader, or unusual fonts, or icons / seals. Reference style isn’t consistent and the footnoted ones have a big gap between reference number and title. Ability to direct-download to CSV would be convenient.

text:
Assignment 4: rVest
Use rvest_wiki01.R to scrape Foreign reserve data from Wikipedia.
Modifying the function to scrape any given table: something like…

scrape_table <- function(url, xpath_string){

link = read_html(url)
topic <- link %>%

html_nodes(xpath=xpath_string) %>%
html_table()

df <- topic[[1]]
return(df)
}


Get the list of countries in the Foreign Reserve table–works, but some of the data are in the wrong format, or otherwise mislabelled. My changes:

Adjusted column names (https://www.statology.org/how-to-rename-data-frame-columns-in-r/)
Removed rows with non-country text (https://www.statology.org/remove-rows-in-r/)
Got rid of “reference” column (https://www.statology.org/remove-columns-in-r/)

Possible Research Plan: this would be fun with Wikipedia track edits (which you could hypothetically iterate over using the “view page history” function). Finding specific points of contention for an article or set of articles, and then using that as a basis either for evidence of coordinated effort or for some qualitative study about historical memory or changing legacies.

title: Assignment Five: some review
text:
If some element of an ER diagram is disconnected, that means there is no key linking it to other elements of the graph (i.e. there’s no path by which to reach it organically).
The cycle of the graph is that “path,” or how you should navigate between different entities in the schema. The sort of cycle the textbook suggests avoiding is one of “cascading prerequisites,” or entities that are connected by multiple cycles.

title: Assignment Five: some review
text:
Question III: Weak entity sets
Weak entity sets solve the problems associated with getting rid of the relationship between two entity sets (i.e. they are now only implicitly related), and only retaining the attributes within the weak entity into its parent entity (no longer uniquely identifiable). With weak entity sets, the identifying relationship makes the entity recognizable, with an explicit relationship to its dependent set, and the ability to participate in other relationships if needed.

title: Assignment Five: some review
text:
Question IV: SQL Syntax

Queries
“ID and name of each employee sho lives in the same city as the location of the company for which the employee works”
SELECT e.ID, e.person_name
FROM employee AS e
JOIN works AS w ON e.ID = w.ID
JOIN company AS c ON w.company_name = c.company_name
WHERE e.city = c.city
“ID and name of each employee who lives in the same city and on the same street as their manager”
SELECT e.ID, e.person_name
FROM employee AS e
JOIN manages AS m ON e.ID = m.ID
JOIN employee AS man ON m.manager_ID = man.ID
WHERE e.street = man.street AND e.city = man.city
NOTE HERE: assuming that “manager” is stored as an employee, i.e. they also have an employee ID that can be easily merged. (Note that I used Claude to explain this distinction).
“ID and name of each employee who earns more than the average salary of all employees of their company”
SELECT e.ID, e.person_name
FROM employee AS e
JOIN works AS w ON e.ID = w.ID
WHERE w.salary > (SELECT avg(salary) FROM works)


SQL Proofing
Running this returns Brandt / Game design twice and Kim’s intro to digital systems once. Per the redundancy with Brandt, it should be SELECT DISTINCT, and capitalization and indentation with NATURAL JOIN is easier to look at in my opinion.
That aside, you end up with way fewer pairings than expected because using “natural join” twice after “from” is recursive, i.e. you end up natural joining the results of a natural join instead of natural joining a pair of elements. There’s also the issue that a professor might teach multiple classes, or multiple professors might teach different sections of the same class, so you probably don’t want to join on sections. The following fix worked for me:
SELECT DISTINCT name, title FROM instructor NATURAL JOIN teaches, course WHERE semester = ‘Spring’ and year = 2017

title: Problem Set IV
text:
Ref: https://www.ripublication.com/ijss16/ijssv11n2_05.pdf and https://psy652.colostate.edu/modules/m13-categorical_predictors.html (with interpretation from AI). Since problem gives 1-0, not -1, this is dummy coding not effect coding.
So y = 10 + 5x + 4s + 3r + 2sr where either sex or region can be 1 or 0. Intercept = 10, slope = 5, e_{s} = 4, e_{r} = 3, e_{sr} = 2
Now you want to rewrite this as y = int + 5 + e_{NM} + e_{NF} + e_{SF}, where NMSF are all 0-1 manifestations of SR (M = 1, N = 1, else 0)
SF: If s,r = 0 then y = 5x + 10 NM: If s,r = 1 then y = 10 + 5x + 4 + 3 + 2 = 5x + 19 NF: If s = 0, r = 1 then y = 10 + 5x + 3 = 5x + 13 ##SM: If s = 1, r = 0 then y = 10 + 5x + 4 = 5x + 14
Note “dummy variable trap”: you can only find effects with a reference group, which should be SM if it’s the one left out of the original model.
5x is constant, intercept is the average of all the groups = (10+19+13+14)/4 = 14, and coefficients are the difference from that average.
SF: 10 - 14 = -4 NM: 19 - 14 = 5 NF: 13 - 14 = -1 SM: 14 - 14 = 0 (this makes sense because it does not appear in the original)
So rewrite as y = 14 + 5x + 5NM - NF - 4SF.
We just recoded the variables, not changed the actual underlying model, so anything we do regression-wise shouldn’t change, including the results of whatever hypothesis test.

title: A6
text:
Look up websites containing the following data representations:
a) Using JSON
b) Using XML
Analyze the websites in terms of structure and composition. Name the technology/methods use for creating the web database.
JSON looks more like SQL as we’ve learnt it, and XML more like the HTML that appears in my GitHub Quarto uploads (they are both “MarkupLanguage” but the relationship is a bit unclear). Certainly, JSON is easier for me to parse; it is also the file format I typically get with APIs or webscraping, which I’ve found pretty readable in R. (https://www.w3schools.com/js/js_json_xml.asp)
It looks like for my use-case, JSON will usually win out because it’s faster, lighter, and more interpretable. But XML is probably relevant for large complex databases, where structural nuances really matter and can better-withstand the data hacking needed to reformat them. This is especially true given that XML has built-in validation through DTD and XSD, which can force data into a structure required for any given professional use-case: legal documents, patient records, anything else where structural inconsistency has significant client-side consequences (https://www.codeitbro.com/blog/json-vs-xml)

title: A6
text:
SQL Query Practice

Rewrite following SQL query without subqueries or set operations: SELECT id FROM student EXCEPT SELECT s id FROM advisor WHERE i.id IS NOT NULL

As written, this says to “return IDs from students, except for students who have an advisor that exists.” In other words, “find students without an advisor,” where you could left-outer-join advisors and students, and just pick the students on the margin (i.e. that have a NULL advisor).
SELECT id
FROM student as s
LEFT OUTER JOIN advisor as a ON s.id = a.s_id
WHERE a.s_id IS NULL

Using the university schema, write an SQL query to find the names and IDs of those instructors who teach every course taught in his or her department (i.e., every course that appears in the course relation with the instructor’s department name). Order result by name.

Hmmm. A few different ways of thinking about this. Exclude instructors that have NOT taught any given course? Instructors whose number of courses taught, equals the number of courses in the department? These are all the subquery, any of them would require joining department with courses with instructors and “teaches.”
Claude fixed my syntax, but logic (expanding outwards from the subquery) is: “find all courses an instructor has taught. Find all the courses in the department. Return professors IDs, only where there are no courses in the department that they have not taught.”
SELECT DISTINCT i.id, i.name
FROM instructor AS i
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
SELECT c.course_id
FROM course AS c
WHERE c.dept_name = i.dept_name
AND c.course_id NOT IN (
SELECT t.course_id
FROM teaches AS t
WHERE t.id = i.id));

Explain the difference between a weak and a strong entity set. Use an example other than the one in Chapter 6 to illustrate. (Consult Ch. 6, 6.5.3)

A strong entity stands on its own and has a primary key–that is, it makes sense as its own table. A weak entity depends on that strong entity and ceases to exist / make sense without it.
As an example, I’m working with legal bills for my final project. An amendment can’t conceptually exist without a bill to attach to. So I have bill-amendment as a weak entity relation in my dataset.
